claim: After more than a decade of sustained success in the fight against malaria, data from 2015 onwards suggests that no significant progress in reducing global malaria cases has been achieved.
source: After more than a decade of sustained success in the fight against malaria, data from 2015 onwards suggests that no significant progress in reducing global malaria cases has been achieved (World malaria report, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to World malaria report, 2019

claim: The rise of insecticide resistance in mosquito vectors and drug resistance in parasites highlights the urgent need to develop new tools if malaria eradication is to remain a viable goal.
source: The rise of insecticide resistance in mosquito vectors and drug resistance in parasites highlights the urgent need to develop new tools if malaria eradication is to remain a viable goal.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about resistance development

claim: Synthetic gene drives spreading by super-Mendelian inheritance within vector populations have been proposed as an area-wide genetic strategy for the control of malaria.
source: Synthetic gene drives spreading by super-Mendelian inheritance within vector populations have been proposed as an area-wide genetic strategy for the control of malaria (Raban et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raban et al., 2020

claim: Gene drives mimic the mechanism of proliferation of a class of naturally occurring selfish genes found in protists, mitochondria, and chloroplasts called homing endonucleases.
source: They mimic the mechanism of proliferation of a class of naturally occurring selfish genes found in protists, mitochondria, and chloroplasts called homing endonucleases and could be deployed to modify the genetic makeup of disease vector populations (Burt, 2003; Windbichler et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burt, 2003 and Windbichler et al., 2011

claim: Proof-of-principle laboratory experiments of CRISPR/Cas9-based gene drives for population suppression have been demonstrated.
source: Proof-of-principle laboratory experiments of CRISPR/Cas9-based gene drives for population suppression, which aims at the elimination of the target population (Kyrou et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2016), as well as population replacement (Gantz et al., 2015; Pham et al., 2019; Adolfi et al., 2020), which aims to spread an anti-malarial trait within a vector population, suggest that these strategies could be deployed to reduce malaria transmission in the field.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kyrou et al., 2018 and Hammond et al., 2016

claim: Proof-of-principle laboratory experiments of CRISPR/Cas9-based gene drives for population replacement have been demonstrated.
source: Proof-of-principle laboratory experiments of CRISPR/Cas9-based gene drives for population suppression, which aims at the elimination of the target population (Kyrou et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2016), as well as population replacement (Gantz et al., 2015; Pham et al., 2019; Adolfi et al., 2020), which aims to spread an anti-malarial trait within a vector population, suggest that these strategies could be deployed to reduce malaria transmission in the field.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gantz et al., 2015; Pham et al., 2019; Adolfi et al., 2020

claim: Few pre-characterized promoter elements driving tissue-specific expression in infection-relevant tissues currently exist in malaria vectors.
source: Few pre-characterized promoter elements driving tissue-specific expression in infection-relevant tissues currently exist in malaria vectors.
evidence: Statement about current state of knowledge in the field

claim: The regulatory elements of the zinc carboxypeptidase A1 (CP), peritrophin1 (Aper1), and vitellogenin (Vg) genes have been reported to drive transgene expression.
source: Examples include the regulatory elements of the zinc carboxypeptidase A1 (CP), peritrophin1 (Aper1), or the vitellogenin (Vg) genes that have been reported to drive transgene expression (Nolan et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2002; Abraham et al., 2005; Nirmala et al., 2006; Volohonsky et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: CP is expressed in the guts of pupae and sugar-fed adults and becomes 10-fold upregulated by blood-feeding as well as by feeding on protein-free meals.
source: CP is expressed in the guts of pupae and sugar-fed adults and becomes 10-fold upregulated by blood-feeding as well as by feeding on protein-free meals, probably triggered by the gut distention (Edwards et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Edwards et al., 1997

claim: CP mRNA levels peak 3 hr post blood-feeding (pbf), with spatial expression limited to the posterior midgut, and return to normal levels 24 hr pbf.
source: Its mRNA levels peak 3 hr post blood-feeding (pbf), with spatial expression limited to the posterior midgut, and return to normal levels 24 hr pbf.
evidence: Follows from citation context about Edwards et al., 1997

claim: Aper1 is only detected in the adult gut, but not in larvae, pupae, or adult carcass.
source: Aper1 is only detected in the adult gut, but not in larvae, pupae, or adult carcass, and its mRNA expression profile is independent of age and blood-feeding (Shen and Jacobs-Lorena, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shen and Jacobs-Lorena, 1998

claim: Aper1 mRNA expression profile is independent of age and blood-feeding.
source: Aper1 is only detected in the adult gut, but not in larvae, pupae, or adult carcass, and its mRNA expression profile is independent of age and blood-feeding (Shen and Jacobs-Lorena, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shen and Jacobs-Lorena, 1998

claim: The Aper1 protein is stored in secretory vesicles and released into the midgut lumen soon after blood meal, where it is cross-linked into the peritrophic matrix via its two tandem domains that bind chitin.
source: The protein is stored in secretory vesicles and released into the midgut lumen soon after blood meal, where it is cross-linked into the peritrophic matrix via its two tandem domains that bind chitin (Devenport et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Devenport et al., 2004

claim: The peritrophic matrix retracts from the midgut wall 48 hr pbf and is excreted after 72 hr pbf.
source: The peritrophic matrix retracts from the midgut wall 48 hr pbf and is excreted after 72 hr pbf (Dinglasan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dinglasan et al., 2009

claim: Alkaline phosphatase 2 (AP2) has a secretion signal and a GPI-anchor and is detected in the detergent resistant membrane (DRM) proteome of non-blood-fed adult Anopheles gambiae midguts.
source: Amongst them we chose alkaline phosphatase 2 (AP2, AGAP006400), which has a secretion signal and a GPI-anchor and is detected in the detergent resistant membrane (DRM) proteome of non-blood-fed adult Anopheles gambiae midguts (Parish et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parish et al., 2011

claim: The study established three transgenic strains ScoGFP-CP, ScoGCFP-AP2, and Aper1-ScoGFP in Anopheles gambiae.
source: We established the three transgenic strains ScoGFP-CP, ScoGCFP-AP2, and Aper1-ScoGFP, in the latter case from a single G1 founder (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental results

claim: Sequencing of all individuals within a G1 founder-cage for each strain confirmed that insertion into the genomic locus was precise at all three loci.
source: Sequencing of all individuals within a G1 founder-cage for each strain confirmed that insertion into the genomic locus was precise at all three loci, and no aberrant integration events could be detected.
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results

claim: For all three modified loci, homozygous individuals were viable and fertile and showed no striking fitness defects during rearing and maintenance.
source: However, following sib-mating we found that for all three modified loci, homozygous individuals were viable and fertile and showed no striking fitness defects during rearing and maintenance.
evidence: Direct observation from experiments

claim: The study established markerless strains Sco-CP, ScoG-AP2, and Aper1-Sco by crossing transgenic strains to a vasa-Cre strain.
source: We next crossed all three transgenic strains to a vasa-Cre strain (Volohonsky et al., 2015). We hereby established the markerless strains Sco-CP, ScoG-AP2, and Aper1-Sco (Figure 2A), all of which were also found to be homozygous viable and fertile.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental results

claim: All three markerless strains were found to be homozygous viable and fertile.
source: We hereby established the markerless strains Sco-CP, ScoG-AP2, and Aper1-Sco (Figure 2A), all of which were also found to be homozygous viable and fertile.
evidence: Direct observation from experiments

claim: For all three markerless strains, precise splicing of the artificial intron occurs and the removal of the artificial intron restores the open reading frame required for expression of both the effector protein and the host gene product.
source: RT-PCRs over the splice junctions and subsequent sequencing confirmed that for all three markerless strains precise splicing occurs and that the removal of the artificial intron restores the open reading frame required for expression of both the effector protein and the host gene product (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Evidence of full-length transcripts and successful splicing was found even in the strains retaining the marker cassette which includes the bidirectional SV40 terminator.
source: However, we found evidence of full-length transcripts and successful splicing (possibly at reduced levels) even in the strains retaining the marker cassette which includes the bidirectional SV40 terminator (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: No significant difference in the level of Scorpine mRNA expression was found when comparing the ScoGFP-CP and Aper1-ScoGFP with their respective markerless lines Sco-CP and Aper1-Sco.
source: Using the Scorpine primers, no significant difference in the level of mRNA expression was found when comparing the ScoGFP-CP and Aper1-ScoGFP with their respective markerless lines Sco-CP and Aper1-Sco (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3C

claim: A significant increase in Scorpine expression was observed for strain ScoG-AP2 following removal of the fluorescent marker-module.
source: A significant increase in expression was observed for strain ScoG-AP2 following removal of the fluorescent marker-module although overall expression levels were substantially lower when compared to the other two strains (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Host gene expression in strains ScoGFP-CP and Sco-CP is not significantly different when compared to the wild type.
source: Our analysis showed that host gene expression in strains ScoGFP-CP and Sco-CP is not significantly different when compared to the wild type.
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis described in the text

claim: The expression of AP2 and Aper1 is significantly reduced by the presence of the transgene including the marker cassette.
source: The expression of AP2 and Aper1 is significantly reduced by the presence of the transgene including the marker cassette.
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis described in the text

claim: Removal of the marker-module significantly restored host gene expression to approximately half of the level observed in the wild type in strain Aper1-Sco.
source: Removal of the marker-module significantly restored host gene expression to approximately half of the level observed in the wild type in strain Aper1-Sco but remained below 10% for strain ScoG-AP2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D

claim: High-confidence peptides for both CP and Aper1 genes were detected in the Sco-CP and Aper1-Sco strains by mass-spectrometry.
source: We detected high-confidence peptides for both genes in the Sco-CP and Aper1-Sco strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Females of the strains including the marker-module showed no statistically significant difference in fecundity compared to G3 wild type.
source: While females of the strains including the marker-module showed no statistically significant difference compared to G3, the markerless strains Sco-CP, ScoG-AP2, and Aper1-Sco laid a significantly reduced number of eggs.
evidence: Supported by fecundity assay data

claim: The markerless strains Sco-CP, ScoG-AP2, and Aper1-Sco laid a significantly reduced number of eggs compared to G3 wild type.
source: While females of the strains including the marker-module showed no statistically significant difference compared to G3, the markerless strains Sco-CP, ScoG-AP2, and Aper1-Sco laid a significantly reduced number of eggs.
evidence: Supported by fecundity assay data

claim: ScoGCFP-AP2 and Aper1-Sco strains showed a statistically significant reduction in the hatching rate compared to the G3 wild type.
source: ScoGCFP-AP2 and Aper1-Sco strains additionally showed a statistically significant reduction in the hatching rate compared to the G3 wild type (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by hatching rate data shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: No significant deviations from an expected 1:1 sex ratio were found for any of the markerless transgenic strains.
source: Since all three modified host genes are female and midgut specific, and because fitness effects would be expected to be sex-specific, we also measured pupal sex ratio of the markerless strains but found no significant deviations from an expected 1:1 sex ratio for any of the transgenics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sex ratio data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Strains ScoGCFP-AP2 and Aper1-ScoGFP did not show a significant effect on P. falciparum oocyst intensity or prevalence.
source: We did not observe a significant effect on oocyst intensity or prevalence in strains ScoGCFP-AP2 and Aper1-ScoGFP (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by SMFA data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Strain ScoGFP-CP showed a significant reduction in P. falciparum infection prevalence.
source: Interestingly, strain ScoGFP-CP showed a significant reduction in infection prevalence (IP; Figure 5A), whereas strain Sco-CP, on the contrary, showed a significantly enhanced level of infection by both measures (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by SMFA data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Strain Sco-CP showed a significantly enhanced level of P. falciparum infection by both intensity and prevalence measures.
source: Interestingly, strain ScoGFP-CP showed a significant reduction in infection prevalence (IP; Figure 5A), whereas strain Sco-CP, on the contrary, showed a significantly enhanced level of infection by both measures (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by SMFA data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Expression of two A. gambiae carboxypeptidase B genes is upregulated upon P. falciparum infection and antibodies against one of them blocked parasite development.
source: It had previously been shown that expression of two A. gambiae carboxypeptidase B genes is upregulated upon P. falciparum infection and that antibodies against one of them blocked parasite development (Lavazec et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lavazec et al., 2007

claim: Strains ScoG-AP2 and Aper1-Sco both showed a significant reduction in P. falciparum oocysts in both infection prevalence and intensity.
source: Strains ScoG-AP2 and Aper1-Sco both showed a significant reduction in P. falciparum oocysts (Figure 5B) in both IP and intensity.
evidence: Supported by SMFA data shown in Figure 5B

claim: A homing rate of 95.95% was calculated for ScoGFP-CP when crossed to a vasa-Cas9 strain.
source: We calculated a homing rate of 95.95% and 98.43% for ScoGFP-CP and Aper1-ScoGFP, respectively, with slightly higher rates in females compared to males (Table S5).
evidence: Supported by homing assay data

claim: A homing rate of 98.43% was calculated for Aper1-ScoGFP when crossed to a vasa-Cas9 strain.
source: We calculated a homing rate of 95.95% and 98.43% for ScoGFP-CP and Aper1-ScoGFP, respectively, with slightly higher rates in females compared to males (Table S5).
evidence: Supported by homing assay data

claim: Strain ScoGCFP-AP2 reached a homing efficiency of 87.78%.
source: Strain ScoGCFP-AP2 reached a homing efficiency of 87.78%.
evidence: Supported by homing assay data

claim: Homozygous strain ScoG-AP2 showed near complete homing of 94.98% with 503 out of 516 individuals inheriting the ScoG-AP2 allele.
source: We recorded near complete homing of 94.98% with 503 out of 516 individuals inheriting the ScoG-AP2 allele.
evidence: Supported by PCR genotyping data

claim: The difference in homing rate between ScoG-AP2 and ScoGCFP-AP2 was not statistically significant.
source: Although this is an improvement compared to the homing rate of ScoGCFP-AP2, the difference was not statistically significant (t-test, p=0.1670).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: For 73 out of 93 non-fluorescent individuals from ScoGCFP-AP2 crosses, a 2 kb product in addition to the wild-type amplicon was detected, suggesting the construct was present but carried rearrangements likely the result of recombination between the GFP and CFP coding sequences.
source: For 73 out of 93 individuals analysed by primers spanning the entire locus, we detected a 2 kb product in addition to the wild-type amplicon. Sequencing of these PCR products suggested the construct was present but carried rearrangements that were likely the result of recombination between the GFP and CFP coding sequences (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B

claim: For ScoGFP-CP, 92% of the sequenced non-fluorescent individuals carried point-mutations or indels.
source: For ScoGFP-CP, 92% of the sequenced non-fluorescent individuals carried point-mutations or indels (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B

claim: All nine non-fluorescent individuals obtained from the experiments with Aper1-ScoGFP retained the wild-type configuration.
source: In contrast, all nine non-fluorescent individuals obtained from the experiments with Aper1-ScoGFP retained the wild-type configuration (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B

claim: In the progeny from crosses with female transhemizygotes the percentage of modified alleles was 73.7% for CP, 92.5% for AP2, and 86.0% for Aper1.
source: In the progeny from crosses with female transhemizygotes the percentage of modified alleles was 73.7% for CP, 92.5% for AP2%, and 86.0% for Aper1, suggesting a significant effect of maternal deposition of Cas9 as previously described for the vasa promoter (Papathanos et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by amplicon sequencing data

claim: In the offspring deriving from male transhemizygotes, 17.2% modified reads were observed for CP, 37.2% for AP2, and 11.2% for Aper1.
source: In the offspring deriving from male transhemizygotes, we observed that the percentage of modified reads in the progeny was substantially lower than in the female cross but higher than expected if no Cas9 carryover or somatic Cas9 activity is assumed to occur. We observed 17.2% modified reads for CP (against an expected maximum of 7.3% if activity is assumed to be restricted to the germline), 37.2% for AP2 (expected 7.6%), and 11.2% for Aper1 (expected 1.7%), suggesting embryonic Cas9 activity occurs in all three strains.
evidence: Supported by amplicon sequencing data

claim: At the CP locus, cleavage occurs upstream of the start codon and the majority of modifications were predicted to only affect the 5' UTR.
source: At the CP locus, cleavage occurs upstream of the start codon and the majority of modifications were predicted to only affect the 5' UTR.
evidence: Based on analysis of sequencing data and prediction of effects

claim: At the AP2 locus, cleavage occurs downstream from the ATG, and hence the modifications observed are predicted to result in frameshifts or the loss of the start codon.
source: In contrast, cleavage of AP2 occurs downstream from the ATG, and hence the modifications observed are predicted to result in frameshifts or the loss of the start codon.
evidence: Based on analysis of sequencing data and prediction of effects

claim: At the Aper1 locus, the cut site is located 19 bases upstream of the STOP codon, and in-frame mutations would affect the terminal amino acids only, whereas frameshifts were predicted to lead either to a premature STOP or to the addition of 25 or 26 C-terminal amino acids.
source: At the Aper1 locus the effector was fused to the 3' end of the coding sequence and the cut site is located 19 bases upstream of the STOP codon. The observed in-frame mutations (22.2% and 31.4% in paternal and maternal crosses) would thus affect the terminal amino acids only, whereas frameshifts were predicted to lead either to a premature STOP or to the addition of 25 (frame +2) or 26 (frame +3) C-terminal amino acids.
evidence: Based on analysis of sequencing data and prediction of effects

claim: All strains including those carrying the entire fluorescent marker genes were found to be homozygous viable and fertile and showed no noticeable fitness cost during standard rearing conditions.
source: Unexpectedly, all strains including those carrying the entire fluorescent marker genes were found to be homozygous viable and fertile and showed no noticeable fitness cost during standard rearing conditions.
evidence: Direct observation from experiments

claim: RNA expression analysis indicated that host gene expression had been reduced in strains ScoGCFP-AP2 and Aper1-ScoGFP carrying the full insert including the fluorescent marker.
source: RNA expression analysis indicated that host gene expression had indeed been reduced in strains ScoGCFP-AP2 and Aper1-ScoGFP carrying the full insert including the fluorescent marker.
evidence: Supported by RNA expression analysis described earlier

claim: The ftz intron can accommodate the A. gambiae U6 promoter and the gRNAs for gene drive and remains functional in mosquitoes.
source: Our data here show similarly that the ftz intron can accommodate the A. gambiae U6 promoter and the gRNAs for gene drive and remains functional in mosquitoes.
evidence: Based on experimental results showing successful splicing and gene drive

claim: The splicing was precise, in the context of Scorpine (AAG-intron-GG) or when inserted within Scorpine::GFP (AGG-intron-AG).
source: The splicing was precise, in the context of Scorpine (AAG-intron-GG) or when inserted within Scorpine::GFP (AGG-intron-AG).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data

claim: When provided with a source of Cas9 in the male or female germline, all gRNA transgenes were able to induce high rates of gene drive of the modified loci.
source: When we provided a source of Cas9 in the male or female germline, all gRNA transgenes were able to induce high rates of gene drive of the modified loci.
evidence: Supported by homing assay data

claim: The minimal, markerless locus ScoG-AP2 outperformed ScoGCFP-AP2 in homing efficiency although the difference was not statistically significant.
source: In the case of the AP2 locus we found that the minimal, markerless locus ScoG-AP2 outperformed ScoGCFP-AP2 although the difference was not statistically significant.
evidence: Supported by homing assay data and statistical analysis

claim: Aberrant homing events were observed in the ScoGCFP-AP2 strain, which are likely the result of recombination between the GFP and CFP coding sequences.
source: We observed aberrant homing events in the latter strain, which are likely the result of recombination between the GFP and CFP coding sequences.
evidence: Supported by PCR and sequencing data

claim: Modifications of endogenous genes could have unforeseen consequences, as observed in the case of the zinc carboxypeptidase A1 (CP) where modifications are possibly directly altering infection outcomes.
source: Our analysis suggested however that modifications of endogenous genes could also have unforeseen consequences. In the case of the zinc carboxypeptidase A1 (CP) we found that modifications of the host gene are possibly directly altering infection outcomes.
evidence: Based on infection assay results

claim: The reduced infection level observed for strain ScoGFP-CP which may express reduced levels of CP protein is consistent with reports on other carboxypeptidase genes.
source: The reduced infection level observed for strain ScoGFP-CP which may express reduced levels of CP protein is consistent with reports on other carboxypeptidase genes (Lavazec et al., 2007; VenkatRao et al., 2017; Raz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations and comparison with published data

claim: Scorpine had previously shown to reduce Plasmodium survival when expressed via different routes in the mosquito midgut.
source: Scorpine was chosen for our study as a prototypical effector molecule as it had previously shown to reduce Plasmodium survival (Fang et al., 2011; Bongio and Lampe, 2015; Wang et al., 2012; Shane et al., 2018) when expressed via different routes in the mosquito midgut.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Modifications of the host genes AP2 and Aper1 did not appear to alter P. falciparum infection levels on their own.
source: Modifications of the host genes AP2 and Aper1 did not appear to alter infection levels on their own.
evidence: Based on infection assay results

claim: The regulatory burden for importing or generating non-autonomous effector strains would be expected to be much lower than strains capable of full gene drive.
source: Importantly, the regulatory burden for importing or generating such non-autonomous effector strains would be expected to be much lower than strains capable of full gene drive and hence, simplify advanced stages of testing against polymorphic isolates of the P. falciparum parasite in the endemic setting without the need for strict containment or geographical isolation.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about regulatory requirements

claim: Non-autonomous effector strains can be established and maintained as true-breeding strains, unlike suppression drives where this is impossible.
source: Since they are incapable of autonomous gene drive, they can be established and maintained, unlike suppression drives where this is impossible, as true-breeding strains.
evidence: Based on experimental results and logical reasoning

claim: The study generated transformation constructs consisting of homology arms for three loci designed to facilitate integration of the Scorpine coding sequence within each gene.
source: We generated transformation constructs consisting of homology arms for these three loci designed to facilitate integration of the Scorpine coding sequence within each gene.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental methods

claim: In the case of CP and AP2, the Scorpine coding sequence was inserted at the start codon and linked to the coding sequence of the host gene via the 2A autocleavage peptide.
source: In the case of CP and AP2, the Scorpine coding sequence was inserted at the start codon and linked to the coding sequence of the host gene via the 2A autocleavage peptide (de Felipe and Ryan, 2004).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design

claim: The effector was anchored to the peritrophic matrix via a C-terminal fusion to Aper1.
source: In contrast, we anchored the effector to the peritrophic matrix via a C-terminal fusion to Aper1.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design

claim: In the AP2 strain, Scorpine is expressed as a GFP-fusion with the aim to enhance stability of the protein.
source: In the AP2 strain, Scorpine is expressed as a GFP-fusion with the aim to enhance stability of the protein (Bokman and Ward, 1981; Janczak et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design with supporting citations

claim: Each artificial intron harbours a fluorescent marker driven by the 3xP3 promoter, flanked by loxP-sites, and the corresponding guide RNA under the control of the ubiquitous and constitutive Anopheles gambiae U6 promoter.
source: Each artificial intron harbours a fluorescent marker driven by the 3xP3 promoter, flanked by loxP-sites, and the corresponding guide RNA under the control of the ubiquitous and constitutive Anopheles gambiae U6 promoter (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct statement of construct design shown in Figure 1A

claim: Integration of the vector backbone distinguished via the additional DsRed marker was only observed for the AP2 locus in several G1 individuals that were discarded.
source: Integration of the vector backbone distinguished via the additional DsRed marker was only observed for the AP2 locus in several G1 individuals that were discarded (Figure 1C).
evidence: Direct observation from transgenesis experiments shown in Figure 1C

claim: Efficient splicing of the artificial introns would occur only in the absence of the 3xP3-GFP or CFP fluorescent transformation marker genes, as they contain the bidirectional SV40 terminator.
source: We predicted that efficient splicing of the artificial introns would occur only in the absence of the 3xP3-GFP or CFP fluorescent transformation marker genes, as they contain the bidirectional SV40 terminator.
evidence: Based on molecular biology knowledge about terminators

claim: The modification of the host genes is not likely to be the main driver of the observed fitness effects in the markerless strains.
source: The comparison suggests that here the modification of the host genes is not likely to be the main driver of the observed fitness effects.
evidence: Based on comparison of fitness data between marked and markerless strains

claim: Inbreeding effects or the contribution of the KIL background (introduced via crossing to the Cre line) could partially explain the observed reduction in fecundity of the markerless strains.
source: Since the removal of the fluorescent module by itself is unlikely to decrease fitness (or could even marginally improve it), inbreeding effects or the contribution of the KIL background (introduced via crossing to the Cre line) could partially explain the observed reduction in fecundity of the markerless strains.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about potential causes of fitness effects

claim: The Cre strain also showed a significant decrease in fecundity when compared to G3.
source: Indeed, the Cre strain also showed a significant decrease when compared to G3.
evidence: Supported by fecundity assay data

claim: The presence of negative fitness effects of the introduced traits under these or other conditions could not be ruled out by the experiments.
source: Nevertheless, the presence of negative fitness effects of the introduced traits under these or other conditions could not be ruled out by our experiments.
evidence: Acknowledgment of experimental limitations

claim: The observed reduction in host gene expression that occurs in strains ScoGCFP-AP2 and Aper1-ScoGFP had no substantial effect on P. falciparum transmission.
source: This indicated that the observed reduction in host gene expression that occurs in both these strains had no substantial effect on transmission.
evidence: Based on infection assay results

claim: A decrease in CP protein levels in strain ScoGFP-CP could possibly explain the observed reduction in infection prevalence.
source: A decrease in CP protein levels in strain ScoGFP-CP could possibly explain the observed effect.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on infection data and literature

claim: Antibodies against A. stephensi carboxypeptidases A and B significantly reduced the oocyst number of P. berghei and P. falciparum, respectively.
source: Similarly, antibodies against the A. stephensi carboxypeptidases A and B significantly reduced the oocyst number of P. berghei and P. falciparum, respectively (VenkatRao et al., 2017; Raz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to VenkatRao et al., 2017 and Raz et al., 2013

claim: The lower homing rate of ScoGCFP-AP2 was unlikely to be related to pre-existing resistant alleles.
source: Although this locus showed higher variability around the ATG insertion site in the Ag1000G data set (The Anopheles gambiae 1000 Genomes Consortium, 2017), no SNPs had been detected in 24 sequenced individuals from the G3 lab colony (Bioproject Accession PRJNA397539, 2017) suggesting that the lower homing rate was unlikely to be related to pre-existing resistant alleles.
evidence: Based on analysis of population genetic data

claim: Maternal deposition of Cas9 occurs in all three strains.
source: In the progeny from crosses with female transhemizygotes the percentage of modified alleles was 73.7% for CP, 92.5% for AP2%, and 86.0% for Aper1, suggesting a significant effect of maternal deposition of Cas9 as previously described for the vasa promoter (Papathanos et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on amplicon sequencing data and comparison with expected values

claim: Embryonic Cas9 activity occurs in all three strains.
source: We observed 17.2% modified reads for CP (against an expected maximum of 7.3% if activity is assumed to be restricted to the germline), 37.2% for AP2 (expected 7.6%), and 11.2% for Aper1 (expected 1.7%), suggesting embryonic Cas9 activity occurs in all three strains.
evidence: Based on amplicon sequencing data and comparison with expected values

claim: For all three loci small indels at the cut site and towards the 5' end of the gRNA were found to be responsible for the majority of modifications.
source: For all three loci small indels at the cut site and towards the 5' end of the gRNA were found to be responsible for the majority of modifications.
evidence: Based on amplicon sequencing data analysis

claim: The reciprocal crosses showed varying patterns of repair suggesting different repair characteristics in the male and female germline or, alternatively, when repair follows after either germline or zygotic cleavage.
source: Interestingly, the reciprocal crosses showed varying patterns of repair suggesting the different repair characteristics in the male and female germline or, alternatively, when repair follows after either germline or zygotic cleavage.
evidence: Based on comparison of amplicon sequencing data from reciprocal crosses

claim: Establishing and tracking markerless modifications in A. gambiae are challenging and have not been attempted previously.
source: Establishing and tracking markerless modifications in A. gambiae are challenging and have not been attempted previously.
evidence: Statement about the novelty and difficulty of the approach

claim: The study is the first to show how markerless gene drive traits can be constructed in the malaria mosquito.
source: We show for the first time how markerless gene drive traits can be constructed in the malaria mosquito.
evidence: Statement of novelty of the work

claim: The lack of a severe fitness phenotype in strains with reduced host gene expression could be explained by redundancy in the set of digestive enzymes, proteases, phosphatases, and peritrophins expressed in the mosquito midgut.
source: The lack of a severe fitness phenotype could be explained by a certain redundancy in the set of digestive enzymes, proteases, phosphatases, and peritrophins expressed in the mosquito midgut, at least under standard rearing conditions, including a high-quality source of human blood.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on biological knowledge

claim: Even low mRNA levels in conjunction with correct splicing of the entire intron including the marker cassette could have led to protein expression at a sufficient level, so as not to result in a measurable impact on fitness.
source: Alternatively, even low mRNA levels in conjunction with correct splicing of the entire intron including the marker cassette (we found evidence for this occurring in all three genes) could have led to protein expression at a sufficient level, so as not to result in a measurable impact on fitness in our experiments.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on experimental observations

claim: It remains to be seen whether the reduced levels of restored expression observed in the AP2 and Aper1 loci would preclude the use of essential genes to host such IGDs.
source: It remains to be seen whether the reduced levels of restored expression (in the case of AP2 and Aper1 loci) observed in this study would preclude the use of essential genes, for which expression levels are particularly critical, to host such IGDs.
evidence: Statement about future research needs

claim: The intron used in the study derives from the Drosophila melanogaster homeobox transcription factor fushi tarazu (ftz), essential for early embryonic development.
source: The intron we used derives from the Drosophila melanogaster homeobox transcription factor fushi tarazu (ftz), essential for early embryonic development, and we have separately found that a full gRNA transgene can be hosted within this intron (A. Nash, unpublished).
evidence: Statement about the source of the intron with citation to unpublished work

claim: Simple genetic modifications may avoid undesired interactions found in more complex constructs.
source: This highlights that simple genetic modifications may avoid undesired interactions found in more complex constructs.
evidence: Based on observation of recombination events in complex constructs

claim: The interaction of multiple gene drives sharing homologous sequences could lead to unintended outcomes in the field.
source: The interaction of multiple gene drives (sharing homologous sequences such as marker genes, promoters, or terminators) could thus lead to unintended outcomes in the field.
evidence: Speculative statement based on observed recombination

claim: Further studies in population cages could reveal to what degree the observed classes of mutations would be actively selected against, which could favour faithful transmission of the drive.
source: Further studies for example in population cages could thus reveal to what degree the observed classes of mutations (Figure 6C) would be actively selected against, which could favour faithful transmission of the drive (Nash et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculative statement about future research with citation

claim: Non-autonomous effectors could be combined with male-specific gene drives, suppressive gene drives, or autonomous rescue drives.
source: It should be noted that non-autonomous effectors as described herein could also be combined with male-specific gene drives, suppressive gene drives, or autonomous rescue drives and the rate of the formation and the dynamic of selection of functional resistance alleles via these routes would be quite different in each case.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential applications

claim: Overall expression from the AP2 locus was found to be lower when compared to the CP and Aper1 loci.
source: In contrast, AP2 chosen due to differential expression in the female gut has not been described before. In our experiments, overall expression from the AP2 locus was found to be lower when compared to the CP and Aper1 loci, suggesting that AP2 would be less suitable as a host gene or as a transgene promoter for the expression of effectors requiring high levels of protein.
evidence: Based on qPCR expression data

claim: AP2 would be less suitable as a host gene or as a transgene promoter for the expression of effectors requiring high levels of protein.
source: In our experiments, overall expression from the AP2 locus was found to be lower when compared to the CP and Aper1 loci, suggesting that AP2 would be less suitable as a host gene or as a transgene promoter for the expression of effectors requiring high levels of protein.
evidence: Based on expression data and logical inference

claim: Strong promoters might not always be ideal, as the dosage-response curves of other types of effectors may vary significantly.
source: Strong promoters might not always be ideal however, as the dosage-response curves of other types of effectors (e.g. transcriptional modulators) may vary significantly.
evidence: Based on biological knowledge about effector molecules

claim: Co-opting the regulatory elements of endogenous loci directly without prior labour-intensive characterization is a viable approach.
source: Together, our data on all three genes suggest, that co-opting the regulatory elements of endogenous loci directly without prior labour-intensive characterization is a viable approach.
evidence: Based on successful expression from all three loci

claim: There is a dearth of promoters for many infection-relevant tissues such as salivary glands, hemocytes, and fatbody.
source: Since there is a dearth of promoters for many infection-relevant tissues (e.g. salivary glands, hemocytes, fatbody) we propose that this characterization step could be avoided, and effector molecules directly incorporated into mosquito gene loci and mobilized by non-autonomous drive.
evidence: Statement about current state of knowledge

claim: Existing RNA expression data sets or enhancer-trap screens could provide a starting point for the identification of suitable genes for hosting effectors.
source: Existing RNA expression data sets or enhancer-trap screens could provide a starting point for the identification of suitable genes (Reid et al., 2018).
evidence: Suggestion based on available resources with citation

claim: The CP locus may not be a suitable host gene for gene drives due to its effect on infection levels.
source: In contrast, strain Sco-CP showed a positive effect on infection levels which would suggest that the CP locus may not be a suitable host gene for gene drives.
evidence: Based on infection assay results

claim: The moderate effects on transmission observed in different directions call for further transmission studies with these strains.
source: Overall, the moderate effects on transmission we observed in different directions in our pilot experiments call for further transmission studies with these strains in order to determine whether Scorpine has realistic potential as an antimalarial effector and to lend further support to the suitability of the three mosquito genes to host effector molecules.
evidence: Statement about need for future research based on current results

claim: Both genetic polymorphisms linked to the modified loci in these inbred strains and the effect of the genetic backgrounds used could influence parasite infections.
source: Both genetic polymorphisms linked to the modified loci in these inbred strains and the effect of the genetic backgrounds used could influence parasite infections and our transmission experiments were not designed to distinguish these effects in full.
evidence: Acknowledgment of experimental limitations

claim: Determining the effect of these modifications on later stages of parasite development using molecular assays is necessary to obtain a full picture.
source: In addition, determining the effect of these modifications on later stages of parasite development using molecular assays is also necessary to obtain a full picture.
evidence: Statement about future research needs

claim: Strains ScoGFP-CP, ScoGCFP-AP2, and Aper1-ScoGFP could be used to isolate defined NHEJ and knockout alleles of the three host genes and characterize their effect on transmission and fitness.
source: Strains ScoGFP-CP, ScoGCFP-AP2, and Aper1-ScoGFP could also be used to isolate defined NHEJ and knockout alleles of the three host genes and characterize their effect on transmission and fitness.
evidence: Suggestion for future experiments

claim: Such studies will likely be required to demonstrate the safety of this and related approaches utilizing host genes.
source: Such studies will likely be required to demonstrate the safety of this and related approaches utilizing host genes.
evidence: Statement about regulatory and safety requirements

claim: The strategy and selected host genes allow for the insertion and direct comparisons of a range of different antimalarial effectors either by secretion into the gut or by anchoring these molecules in the peritrophic matrix.
source: In summary, the strategy and the selected host genes we have presented here now allow for the insertion and direct comparisons of a range of different antimalarial effectors either by secretion into the gut or by anchoring these molecules in the peritrophic matrix.
evidence: Summary statement based on experimental results

claim: The most significant knowledge gap regarding transmission blocking modifications is to what degree effects observed with lab strains of P. falciparum would be reproducible using circulating parasites or under field conditions.
source: The most significant knowledge gap, when it comes to transmission blocking modifications of transgenic mosquitoes, is to what degree any effects observed with lab strains of P. falciparum would be reproducible using circulating parasites isolated from patient blood or would hold up under actual field conditions which could wildly differ from standard laboratory experiments.
evidence: Statement about current limitations in the field

claim: Non-autonomous effector strains can be established and maintained as true-breeding strains, unlike suppression drives.
source: Since they are incapable of autonomous gene drive, they can be established and maintained, unlike suppression drives where this is impossible, as true-breeding strains.
evidence: Based on experimental results and biological knowledge

claim: The regulatory burden for importing or generating non-autonomous effector strains would simplify advanced stages of testing against polymorphic isolates of P. falciparum in endemic settings without the need for strict containment or geographical isolation.
source: Importantly, the regulatory burden for importing or generating such non-autonomous effector strains would be expected to be much lower than strains capable of full gene drive and hence, simplify advanced stages of testing against polymorphic isolates of the P. falciparum parasite in the endemic setting without the need for strict containment or geographical isolation.
evidence: Speculative statement about regulatory implications

claim: When combined with other strains capable of autonomous Cas9 gene drive, these non-autonomous strains could be deployed to contribute to reducing malaria transmission without the need for any further genetic modification.
source: When combined with other strains capable of autonomous Cas9 gene drive, whether designed for replacement or suppression, these strains could then, without the need for any further genetic modification, be deployed to contribute to reducing malaria transmission by mosquito populations in the field.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential field application
